indicators.note: something placed in another thing sits inside it, so one group of letters goes within the other

parts.note: stock as an adjective means standard or usual, as in a stock answer
a copper is a police officer, a PC or police constable
a ring is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: A plumber fits a ring of copper inside an ordinary tap.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper and ring look like plumbing materials, but copper is police slang and ring is just a shape; stock as in a stock phrase means standard.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopcock is a valve on a water pipe, turned by hand to stop or start the flow, so it is a kind of tap.

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a kid is a young goat, and twin means two of them

explanation.surface: An antelope is raising a pair of twin goats as its own young.
explanation.walkthrough: Raising sounds like bringing up young, but in a down entry it turns KID KID upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: The dik-dik is a very small African antelope, named for the alarm call it gives.

clue.text: Cheeky thing south of London in song on the radio?

indicators.note: radio is heard rather than read, so what follows is judged by its sound alone

parts.note: the song Londonderry Air; below London in the title, as this is a down clue, come the words Derry Air

explanation.surface: A cheeky item heard on the radio, a song about somewhere south of London.
explanation.walkthrough: South of London is not a place like Brighton: in a down entry it means the words that follow London in the Irish song title Londonderry Air, the tune of Danny Boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A derriere is a polite French-derived word for the buttocks, and the cheeks are the bottom, hence a cheeky thing.

clue.text: With article breaking, bear in mind it could be — ours?

definitions.note: a cryptic, example-style definition: what is made in Britain could be ours from a British setter's view

indicators.note: something breaking falls apart, so these letters are smashed and reassembled in a new order

parts.note: A is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: Remember, with the item now broken, it might well be something of ours.
explanation.walkthrough: Bear in mind looks like an instruction to remember, but it is the anagram material, together with IT and the article A.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter writes for a British paper, so goods labelled as manufactured in the United Kingdom could be described as ours.

indicators.note: a version of something is a reworked form of it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the printed word splits in two: its first three letters join the fodder and the rest is the signal

explanation.surface: An autocratic state faces genuine subversion from its opponents.
explanation.walkthrough: Subversion reads as one word about plotting against the regime, but it has to be cut in two, and the question mark admits the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Belarus has been ruled by one strongman president for decades, so the country serves as an example of autocratic rule.

clue.text: Give-and-take retailer was ruined, old man keeping quiet

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds the other inside

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: A shop that went under, its elderly owner staying silent about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Old man is a father, not an elderly man. Swap Shop was also a much-loved BBC children's TV show where viewers traded toys.
explanation.definitionFit: A swap shop is a place where goods are exchanged rather than bought, so trading there is a matter of give-and-take.

clue.text: Obstacle in hollow filled with French earth

indicators.note: a thing filled with something has that something inside it

parts.note: a dent is a small hollow in a surface
terre is the French word for earth

explanation.surface: A barrier stands in a hole that has been packed with soil from France.
explanation.walkthrough: Hollow looks like an adjective but is a noun here, a small depression in a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A deterrent is something that discourages or blocks an action, so it serves as an obstacle or hindrance.

clue.text: Possible couch potato internalising variety of woes

indicators.note: to internalise is to take inside oneself, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: tater is a colloquial word for potato

indicators.note: a variety offers a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A couch potato bottling up all kinds of troubles.
explanation.walkthrough: Couch potato is a set phrase for a lazy viewer, but it must be split: couch belongs to the definition and potato to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sofa built for two people is called by this name, so a couch could be one.

clue.text: Stern, say, man with strap-on locks

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing put on another is added straight after it

parts.note: a thick, bushy mass of hair is a word for a mass of locks
an athletic man, the sort who wears a jockstrap

explanation.surface: A stern-looking man with a strap-on hairpiece.
explanation.walkthrough: Stern is not an adjective but the American radio presenter Howard Stern, and strap-on is a saucy red herring split into strap and on.
explanation.definitionFit: Howard Stern is a radio host famous for provocative talk, the textbook example of a presenter who sets out to offend listeners.

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so these letters are messed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Was that old wine awful? Not half! is a British exclamation meaning very much so.
explanation.walkthrough: Not half looks like the end of the exclamation, but NOT belongs to the anagram letters and half alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A proportion of one out of every two equals fifty per cent, exactly a half.

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short, so it loses its final letter
to shelter something is to keep it inside, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: olive is a shade of green; shortened, it loses its last letter
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone called Olive briefly gives cover to a blackbird.
explanation.walkthrough: Olive looks like a woman's name, but it is a colour; black bird reads as blackbird, yet black is only B.
explanation.definitionFit: A grebe is a diving water bird with lobed feet, common on lakes.

parts.note: surface reading: the outcome of a game of football, oddly hyphenated; setter's reading: the hyphen sits between two Os, showing the scoreline nil-nil inside the word

explanation.walkthrough: Some hints that part of the word matters: hidden in it, the stray hyphen makes O-O, how a 0-0 score is written. No letters of the answer are hidden, so this is a cryptic definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A match finishing nil-nil has no scoring by either side and ends level, which is exactly what the phrase describes.

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, and with that gone the final letter is dropped

parts.note: A former US president; without his last letter

explanation.surface: Wait a moment, the former leader has turned tail and left!
explanation.walkthrough: Back's gone sounds like someone retreating, but it means BIDEN, the former US president, loses his last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To bide is an old word for waiting or remaining, still heard in the phrase bide your time.

clue.text: Emperor's new clothes, third stuffed into brown case

indicators.note: put into something, a piece goes inside it

parts.note: bay is a reddish-brown colour, especially of horses

indicators.note: something stuffed is wrecked or done for, so these letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a lawsuit, a case in court

explanation.surface: The emperor's new clothes, packed into a brown suitcase for the third time.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown case wants to be a suitcase, but it is two separate pieces, a horse colour and a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fairy tale the emperor's invisible new clothes leave him naked, dressed only in the skin he was born in.

clue.text: Where something latched onto about programme leaves producer?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: a feeding baby or young animal latches onto a nipple
a programme is a plan of action

explanation.surface: A TV programme that a producer leaves, something having stuck to it.
explanation.walkthrough: Programme leaves producer reads like someone quitting a show; split it, and leaves producer is a plant that yields leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The tea plant is the shrub Camellia sinensis, grown for the foliage that is dried to brew the drink.

clue.text: Flag in Spain gone with TV broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so these letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A national flag in Spain has vanished from the television coverage.
explanation.walkthrough: Flag is not a banner but a flagstone; broadcast sits well with TV, which is why it disguises the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A flag, short for flagstone, is a flat slab used for pavements, the same thing as a slab laid on a path.

indicators.note: talking is speech, so what matters is how the word is pronounced

parts.note: done means finished, as in we are through

explanation.surface: A theatre cast that has finished speaking its lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast looks like a noun, the actors; it is the past tense of the verb meaning to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast and threw are both past tenses of verbs meaning to fling or hurl something.

clue.text: Vulgar, a word that's void in essay

indicators.note: placed in something, a piece goes inside it

parts.note: an essay is an attempt, a try
taken as written

indicators.note: a void thing is emptied, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: the word emptied of its middle

explanation.surface: A vulgar essay, one in which a word means nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Essay here is the old sense of an attempt, not a piece of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tawdry means cheap, showy and lacking in taste, which is close to coarse or vulgar.

clue.text: Bunfight that's sickening ends it a fitting way?

indicators.note: what ends something comes last, so this part follows the other

parts.note: it in the sense of sex appeal, abbreviated SA
vile means disgusting or sickening
a bunfight is a heated quarrel, a row

explanation.surface: A nasty squabble brings everything to a fitting close.
explanation.walkthrough: A vile row ends IT: so SA comes first. Savile Row is the London street famous for bespoke tailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Tailors measure clients for suits there, so the street is a way, or road, where fittings happen.

clue.text: Grant for example cut, according to dictator?

indicators.note: a dictator here is someone dictating aloud for a secretary, so the word is taken as heard

parts.note: to hew is to cut or chop

explanation.surface: A grant has been cut on a dictator's orders.
explanation.walkthrough: Grant looks like a sum of money and dictator a tyrant; Grant is the actor, and the dictator is someone dictating a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Grant is the English film actor, so his first name is an instance of a man named Grant.

clue.text: Might her inattentive husband be, reportedly, playing around?

definitions.text: Might her inattentive husband be, reportedly, playing around?

parts.words: Might her inattentive husband be, reportedly, playing around?
parts.note: surface reading: a neglected wife suspects her husband of having an affair; setter's reading: playing around said out loud is playing a round, the unit of a game on the links

explanation.walkthrough: Reportedly signals the sound pun: around is a round, eighteen holes of the sport, not infidelity.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a wife left alone for long hours because her husband is always out on the course.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: clotted cream famously comes from Cornwall
second meaning, read cryptically: like corn, a cereal grain, with the suffix ish

explanation.surface: Is the cream a little grainy, as cream sometimes can be?
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a made-up word split as CORN-ISH, which the question mark flags. Cornwall is the county at England's south-western tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream from Cornwall is a regional speciality, and corn plus ish jokingly means somewhat like grain.

clue.text: Percentage of litre, a clear, sweet liquid

indicators.note: a percentage is a portion of a whole, so the letters are a run inside the following words

parts.note: the run spans the end of the first word, the article, and the start of the last

explanation.surface: Measuring what share of a litre of clear liquid is sugary.
explanation.walkthrough: Percentage reads as a number, but it only means part of the following words.
explanation.definitionFit: Treacle is a thick sugary syrup made in refining sugar, which British cooks use in tarts and puddings.
